catalog_quote: Stress is unpredictable in Wersing, but Schapper and Hendery (2014) had not identified stress-differentiated minimal pairs at the time of publication. Since then, I have noted some, but the number remains small: (1) /aˈmi/ ‘breast’ ≠ /ˈami/ ‘there’; /aˈmuiŋ/ ‘submerge’ ≠ /ˈamuiŋ/ ‘cape’; /aˈtok/ ‘your stomach’ ≠ /ˈatok/ ‘peck, lunge at’; /suˈak/ ‘prawn’ ≠ /ˈsuak/ ‘store sharp object’. Given the low functional load stress carries, I do not mark stress in the practical orthography used here. The reader can check where stress falls in the “Pronunciation” field of each entry. ... The low functional load carried by stress today in Wersing is partly due to very many historically pre-tonic vowels being lost from original initial CV syllables.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically specified and not predictable from the segmental string; it is contrastive (a handful of minimal pairs such as aˈmi 'breast' vs ˈami 'there'), though its functional load is low because historical loss of pretonic vowels removed many pre-stress syllables. Stress is recorded per lexeme in the dictionary's Pronunciation field (in practice it falls on the final or penultimate syllable of roots, occasionally earlier). Some prefixes interact with stress: derivational na- attracts stress (ˈnatutuk 'inform'), while person-agreement prefixes on C-initial roots surface as unstressed Cè- syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Prefix /na-/ attracts stress (footnote 2: /ˈnatutuk/ 'inform'); Series I agreement prefixes surface as an unstressed CV syllable with epenthetic vowel; epenthetic cluster-breaking vowels (written è) are unstressed; a few items show irregular reduction of unstressed vowels to schwa (miˈra ~ məˈra 'inside'); vowel epenthesis across (C)VC.CV(C) roots occurs 'where stress is on the last syllable'; synchronic metathesis affects final unstressed syllables with a high vowel.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern the (root/lexical) word as elicited in citation/list form from a single speaker of the Pureman dialect (Peitoko variant); stress is given for headwords (citation forms) in the Pronunciation field. Author states this 2020 description supersedes Schapper & Hendery 2014 where they differ.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement (Schapper 2020) is based on one speaker of the Peitoko variant of the Pureman dialect (south-east coast of Alor), the same dialect as the Schapper & Hendery 2014 sketch ('Wersing Pureman'); Schapper says the 2020 intro supersedes the 2014 sketch where they differ. Other dialects (Kolana on the east coast, Taramana/Adagai on the north coast, Maritaing) are not separately described for stress; Stokhof 1975's prominence-marked wordlist is Kolana dialect. All fall under glottocode wers1238.

sources.citation: Klamer, Marian (ed.). 2017. The Alor-Pantar languages: History and typology. Second edition. (Studies in Diversity Linguistics 3.) Berlin: Language Science Press.
sources.note: Ch.2 (Holton & Robinson) p.54: 'In most of the modern languages stress is on the penultimate syllable; however, stress may also be attracted to heavy syllables, as in Teiwa ji'var' -- family-level remark, not Wersing-specific. Ch.3 (Schapper, Huber & van Engelenhoven) p.122: in Wersing historically short unstressed vowels were lost (tlam < pAP *tala:m 'six'). No Wersing stress rule.
Consonant and vowel phoneme tables only (citing Schapper & Hendery 2014); nothing on stress.
